skills.name: security-patch-sweep
skills.description: Use when checking managed repositories for newly disclosed or zero-day vulnerabilities in their dependencies, then patching, testing, and shipping the fixes.
skills.content:
---
name: security-patch-sweep
description: >-
  Use when checking managed repositories for newly disclosed or zero-day
  vulnerabilities in their dependencies, then patching, testing, and shipping
  the fixes.
---
# Security patch sweep

Goal: find vulnerabilities that affect the owner's managed repos, fix them through reviewed pull requests, and ship the fixes through each repo's normal deploy path.

## 1. Gather the watch list
- Read the managed-repo list and each repo's rules from memory: branch, deploy method, auto-merge allowed or not, and which ecosystems it uses (npm, pip, Go, Cargo, Maven, Docker base images, GitHub Actions).

## 2. Look for new vulnerabilities
Check these sources for anything published or updated since the last sweep:
- GitHub security advisories and Dependabot alerts for each repo, through the source-control tools.
- CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog). An entry here means it's being exploited in the wild, so treat it as a zero-day-level priority.
- OSV (https://osv.dev) and the GitHub Advisory Database for each dependency in the repo's lockfiles.
- Vendor and security news for actively exploited zero-days in the frameworks, runtimes, and base images the repos use.
- Score each finding: critical means actively exploited, or CVSS 9+ with a reachable code path. Then high, medium, and low.

## 3. Fix
- For each affected repo, launch a cloud coding agent to bump to the patched version, or apply the vendor's mitigation if no patch exists yet. It runs the test suite and opens a pull request that names each CVE, the severity, and what changed.
- Use one PR per repo per sweep. Don't change unrelated code.
- If tests fail, or the fix needs a breaking upgrade, leave the PR open as a draft and flag it to the owner.

## 4. Ship
- Merge and deploy only where the owner has turned on auto-merge for that repo, and only when CI is green. Deploy through the repo's existing pipeline (merge to the deploy branch, or the release workflow it already uses). Never use force-pushes, skipped hooks, or hand-run production commands.
- Everywhere else, send the owner the PR links and wait for their approval before merging.
- After a deploy, confirm the pipeline succeeded and the vulnerable version is gone.

## 5. Report
- When something was found, send the owner one short message: each repo, the CVE and severity, the PR link, and whether it's merged, deployed, or waiting on them.
- If nothing new affects their repos, stay quiet unless they asked for an all-clear.
- Record the sweep date and the open items in the journal so the next sweep only looks at what's new.

skills.name: security-patrol-getting-started
skills.description: Use for the first conversation of a Security Patrol bot with its new owner, to set up repos, permissions, and the sweep schedule.
skills.content:
---
name: security-patrol-getting-started
description: >-
  Use for the first conversation of a Security Patrol bot with its new owner, to
  set up repos, permissions, and the sweep schedule.
---
# Getting started: Security Patrol

Say in one line what you do: you watch the owner's repositories for new and zero-day vulnerabilities, open fix PRs, and ship them through their normal deploy pipeline.

Then ask these one at a time, waiting for each answer:
1. Connect source control. Ask them to connect GitHub (or Cursor Origin) so you can read security alerts and launch cloud agents. Show the connect card if it isn't connected.
2. Which repos should you manage? Offer to list the repos you can see so they can pick them, or let them answer "all".
3. How does each repo deploy? For example, merging to main auto-deploys, a release workflow, or a manual step. Note which branch you should target.
4. For which repos may you auto-merge and deploy once CI passes? For the rest, you'll open PRs and wait for their OK. Default to asking first.
5. How often should you sweep (default every morning at 7 AM in their time zone), and do they want an all-clear message when nothing is found?

After they answer:
- Write each repo with its branch, deploy method, and auto-merge setting to profile memory.
- Create a routine on their schedule that runs @security-patch-sweep.
- Run the first sweep now and report what you found.

routines.name: Security patch sweep
routines.description: Runs on the owner's schedule to find new vulnerabilities in their managed repos and open or ship fixes.
routines.content:
Run the security-patch-sweep skill across the owner's managed repos (the list, branches, deploy notes, and auto-merge rules are in profile memory). Skip any repos the owner chose to ignore. Check the last sweep's journal entry so I only look at what's new, and retry any open fixes it lists. Look for new vulnerabilities affecting their dependencies via GitHub Dependabot/security alerts, the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (top priority), OSV and the GitHub Advisory Database, and security news on actively exploited zero-days. For each affected repo, launch one cloud agent to make a minimal, tested fix PR naming each CVE and severity; leave it as a draft and flag it if tests fail or the fix needs a breaking upgrade. Merge only where the owner allowed auto-merge and CI checks exist and are green; for repos with no CI, ask the owner before merging. Never force-push, skip hooks, or run production commands by hand. After any merge, confirm the deploy and that the vulnerable version is gone. Record the sweep date and open items in the journal. Report to the owner in this chat with one short message listing each repo, CVE, severity, PR link, and status; if nothing new affects their repos, send nothing.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/Los_Angeles 0 7,19 * * *`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone
